During his twelve years in office, [President](President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Franklin D. Roosevelt](Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") appointed eight new members of the [Supreme Court of the United States](Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States"): [Associate Justices](Associate_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States") [Hugo Black](Hugo_Black "Hugo Black"), [Stanley F. Reed](Stanley_Forman_Reed "Stanley Forman Reed"), [Felix Frankfurter](Felix_Frankfurter "Felix Frankfurter"), [William O. Douglas](William_O._Douglas "William O. Douglas"), [Frank Murphy](Frank_Murphy "Frank Murphy"), [James F. Byrnes](James_F._Byrnes "James F. Byrnes"), [Robert H. Jackson](Robert_H._Jackson "Robert H. Jackson"), and [Wiley Blount Rutledge](Wiley_Blount_Rutledge "Wiley Blount Rutledge"). Additionally, he elevated sitting Justice [Harlan F. Stone](Harlan_F._Stone "Harlan F. Stone") to [chief justice](Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States "Chief Justice of the United States"). Roosevelt's nine nominations filled eight seats on the Supreme Court because Byrnes resigned while Roosevelt was still in office. Roosevelt nominated Rutledge to the seat vacated by Byrnes.

## First term without vacancy

During his first term, Roosevelt did not fill a single Supreme Court vacancy, and the court, led by [the "Four Horsemen"](Four_Horsemen_(Supreme_Court) "Four Horsemen (Supreme Court)") of [Willis Van Devanter](Willis_Van_Devanter "Willis Van Devanter"), [James Clark McReynolds](James_Clark_McReynolds "James Clark McReynolds"), [George Sutherland](George_Sutherland "George Sutherland") and [Pierce Butler](Pierce_Butler_(judge) "Pierce Butler (judge)"), struck down many of his [New Deal](New_Deal "New Deal") programs. One of Roosevelt's most severe political defeats during his presidency was the failure of the [Judicial Procedures Reform Bill of 1937](Judiciary_Reorganization_Bill_of_1937 "Judiciary Reorganization Bill of 1937"), popularly known as the [court-packing](Court-packing "Court-packing") bill, which sought to stack a hostile Supreme Court in his favor by adding more associate justices.[[1]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-1)

## Hugo Black nomination

Soon after this setback, however, Roosevelt obtained his first opportunity to appoint a Supreme Court justice when conservative Van Devanter retired. Roosevelt wanted the replacement to be a "thumping, evangelical New Dealer" who was reasonably young, confirmable by the Senate, and from a region of the country unrepresented on the court.[[2]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-2) The three final candidates were [Solicitor General](Solicitor_General_of_the_United_States "Solicitor General of the United States") [Stanley Forman Reed](Stanley_Forman_Reed "Stanley Forman Reed"), Indiana Senator [Sherman Minton](Sherman_Minton "Sherman Minton"), and Alabama Senator [Hugo Black](Hugo_Black "Hugo Black").[[3]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-Univ4-3) Roosevelt said Reed "had no fire", and Minton didn't want the appointment at the time.[[3]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-Univ4-3) Black was a candidate from the South who as a senator had voted for all twenty-four of Roosevelt's major New Deal programs,[[3]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-Univ4-3) and had been an outspoken advocate of the court-packing plan. Roosevelt admired Black's use of the investigative role of the [Senate](United_States_Senate "United States Senate") to shape the American mind on reforms, his strong voting record, and his early support, which dated back to 1933.[[4]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-4)

On August 12, 1937, Roosevelt nominated Black to fill the vacancy. For the first time since 1853, the Senate departed from its tradition, which had been to confirm the appointment of a sitting senator without debate.[[5]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-Univ6-5) Instead, it referred the nomination to the [Judiciary Committee](United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary "United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary").[[5]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-Univ6-5) Black was criticized by other senators and *<Newsweek>* for his bigotry, his cultural roots, and later when it became public, his [Ku Klux Klan](Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan") membership,[[6]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-University7-6) but the committee recommended Black's confirmation by a vote of 13—4 on August 16.[[7]](Franklin_D._Roosevelt_Supreme_Court_candidates#cite_note-VanDeer1
